posts.content_md:
While searching the recent abstracts on SciFinder, I found the following:

Title: "Modified dichromated gelatin for increasing moisture resistance"

Authors: Romero-Arellano/Solano/Martinez-Ponce

Journal: Revista Mexicana de Fisica (2006), 52(2), 99-103 (in Spanish)

Translated abstract: It is presented a comparison between the diffraction efficiency in holographic phase gratings induced in films prepared with two different mixtures based on dichromated gelatin. The traditional mixture (DCG) is modified incorporating glycerol (DCG-G) before deposition. Both kinds of film were dried under different humidity conditions. It is seen that optical recording on DCG-G films is independent on the moisture settings. Also, the induced refractive index modulation is larger than the one obtained with DCG.

***

I don't have access to this journal, nor would I feel comfortable in translating the Spanish, but the last comment regarding the increased index modulation is interesting. It isn't clear what is meant by "increasing moisture resistance" but maybe it means that sensitivity variations (during exposure) due to moisture content are reduced (?) Does anyone have experience with (or know of references to) glycerol in DCG? I know nothing about it. Jeff's new green sensitive DCG uses it also.

posts.content_md:
> **Joe:** While searching the recent abstracts on SciFinder, I found the following:Title: "Modified dichromated gelatin for increasing moisture resistance"Authors: Romero-Arellano/Solano/Martinez-PonceJournal: Revista Mexicana de Fisica (2006), 52(2), 99-103 (in Spanish)Translated abstract: It is presented a comparison between the diffraction efficiency in holographic phase gratings induced in films prepared with two different mixtures based on dichromated gelatin. The traditional mixture (DCG) is modified incorporating glycerol (DCG-G) before deposition. Both kinds of film were dried under different humidity conditions. It is seen that optical recording on DCG-G films is independent on the moisture settings. Also, the induced refractive index modulation is larger than the one obtained with DCG.***I don't have access to this journal, nor would I feel comfortable in translating the Spanish, but the last comment regarding the increased index modulation is interesting. It isn't clear what is meant by "increasing moisture resistance" but maybe it means that sensitivity variations (during exposure) due to moisture content are reduced (?) Does anyone have experience with (or know of references to) glycerol in DCG? I know nothing about it. Jeff's new green sensitive DCG uses it also.

It's surprising that the addition of glycerol results in an increased index modulation. I am wondering why this is. From the little I gathered, the authors seem to assume it related to a decreased refractive index of the the bulk layer owing to a larger amount of water bound to the glycerol (put aside that glycerol gelatin allows for higher dichromate concentrations). I understand they suggest glycerol favored Cr (V) formation.

As of now the thing seems to be limited to (low spatial frequency) transmission holograms only.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
Thanks, Tom, Colin, and Martin.

The Spanish paper and the babel-fish translation look pretty interesting. I may try to revive my limited knowledge of Spanish, from school-days long ago.

After reading some of the recent literature on DCG, it seems like attention has been focused on the formation of Cr(V) as a "first stage" in the process, the "second stage" being the reduction down to Cr(III).

I think this new "attitude" might bring about some real advances in DCG.

posts.content_md:
> **Joe:** After reading some of the recent literature on DCG, it seems like attention has been focused on the formation of Cr(V) as a "first stage" in the process, the "second stage" being the reduction down to Cr(III).
 

Joe, this whole CrVI CrV and CrIII aspect of DCG has kept me captivated for quite some time, and I have been thinking along those lines for months now. Jeff's G-307 and my statements that there are less greenies with emulsion that has been allowed to set in the fridge for days or weeks then recooked stem from discusssion about that.

It would be nice if Jeff has the time to explain what is going on in the G-307 with each of the chemicals. 

Martin, I too am wonder why they notice an increase in index modulation. With DCG, if it is processed such that there is an Air/Crosslinked Gelatin differential the difference in index of refraction between those two is high compared to a small amount of water that may additionally be in the Crosslinked sites.

Index of refraction of air is 1

Index of refraction of water is 1.33

Index of refraction of Crown Glass is 1.52

Index of refraction of glycerine is 1.47

Index of refraction of set gelatin is 1.31 - 1.5(via three internet search sites of various concentrations of cured but not waterless gelatin concentration mixtures)

Index of refraction of Crosslinked hardened dried gelatin is ???

I would have to say after alcohol drying the index of refraction of gelatin should be around 1.5 or more.

So adding glycerin or water would seem to lower this the the difference of Air/gelatin.

This brings up a very interesting subject. I could not find anywhere what the index of refraction of dried (waterless) gelatin is. It might be a nice experiement.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
The so-called "increased index modulation" in that abstract is perhaps misleading. Maybe all it really means is that diffraction efficiency is increased due to a better differential of hardened/unhardened gelatin, when using their DCG system containing glycerol. In other words, better "sensitivity."

To quote from Jeff's new paper:

"The small amount of glycerol in our sensitizer formulation appears to play a crucial role in enabling the transformation of the light-produced Cr(V) to take place much more rapidly at 100 degrees C. Without glycerol the process seems to take more than a half hour to harden sufficiently. So it may be true to say that hot glycerol catalyses the reaction Cr(V) to Cr(III)."

(...) If the the gelatin is swollen (swollen with water) the index is 1.36. Gelatin containing silver bromide has a refractive index of about 1.62."

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Martin, thank you. I could not find that information anywhere.

Now this is interesting that I never thought about, 

AgBr has an index of refraction of 2.25

AgBr in gelatin (what concentration?) has an index of refraction of 1.62

Gelatin/AmDi with exp and dehydrated has and index of refraction of 1.55

So clearly gelatin with AgBr would have a higher index of refraction then a processed DCG hologram. Now if one could get the air into the unexposed regions, the AgBr (bleached Silver Halide) hologram should be more efficient then DCG.

What is it (hardener) in Silver Halide emulsion that keep the emulsion gelatin from washing away in the unexposed and processed areas?

How can we get AgBr into the exposed areas of a DCG hologram?

How can we get the gelatin out of the unexposed areas of a bleached Silver Halide hologram?
